headline: Moon's Ancient Magnetic Secrets Locked in Tiny Iron Particles
meta_description: Scientists discover a rare form of iron in lunar soil that acts as a magnetic time capsule, preserving clues about the Moon's lost magnetic field.
summary_short: Chang'e-6 lunar samples reveal nanoscale iron particles that may unlock secrets of the Moon's ancient magnetism, opening new windows into our satellite's past.
body:
Chinese researchers have discovered a rare form of metallic iron—called γ-Fe—preserved inside impact-glass particles from the Moon, potentially serving as a microscopic fossil of the Moon's long-lost magnetic field. Led by Prof. Haifeng Du at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, the team found that these nanoscale iron particles can maintain a stable magnetic signal, making them natural recorders of magnetic information from the Moon's ancient past. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on September 16, reveal something unexpected: γ-Fe, which normally exists only at high temperatures on Earth, can survive at the lunar surface under the extreme conditions created by impacts.

The researchers used advanced techniques including focused ion beam preparation and transmission electron microscopy to examine the lunar soil. They discovered that γ-Fe particles could form a stable single-vortex magnetic state and retain consistent magnetic responses when exposed to external fields. This stability is remarkable because it suggests these particles could have preserved magnetic information across millions of years. Dr. Long Li, a team member from the institute, noted that "this tiny magnetic fossil may help us better understand the Moon's ancient magnetic history."

What makes this discovery particularly significant is how it expands our understanding of the Moon's history. Because γ-Fe and another iron form, α-Fe, develop under different conditions and behave differently magnetically, each could potentially record information from separate stages of lunar impact events. The Moon no longer generates a global magnetic field, but these microscopic particles offer a rare window into when it did—and how that protective field changed over billions of years. Future research will determine exactly how much these minerals can reveal about our Moon's vanished magnetism.
quick_facts: Chinese Academy of Sciences discovered rare γ-Fe iron in lunar soil
Found inside impact-glass particles from Chang'e-6 mission samples
Can preserve stable magnetic signals like a microscopic fossil
Published in Proceedings of National Academy of Sciences, September 16
